figures.name: congestion_start_mxsoc_convention
figures.notes: MXSOC's own start convention for the backup: 'Pretty amazing the backup is over after 25 months (we use 15 Oct 2020 as the start)'. The backup 'went from zero to 42 between 15 Oct 2020 to Feb 2021'. This record's event is the 2021 build to the January 2022 peak; the October 2020 start is recorded so the truncation is explicit, not hidden.
figures.source_name: Marine Exchange of Southern California (Capt. Kip Louttit, Executive Director), reported by Port Technology International, 22-23 Nov 2022

figures.name: queue_feb2021_mxsoc_retrospective
figures.notes: 'The backup went from zero to 42 between 15 Oct 2020 to Feb 2021 and then dropped to 9 in June 2021.' Retrospective summary in MXSOC's end-of-backup announcement; month granularity only. A dated point inside the same window (8 Feb 2021) is the separate entry queue_2021-02-08_point_count — the two are not the same day and are not blended.
figures.source_name: Marine Exchange of Southern California, reported by Maritime Magazine (Maritime Mag), Nov 2022
figures.unit: container ships in the backup (waiting for berth), reached between 2020-10-15 and Feb 2021 (month granularity as reported)

figures.name: queue_2021-02-08_point_count
figures.notes: 'the 62 vessels at berth Monday broke a former record – as did 32 containerships at berth... a total of 46 vessels at anchor... Total ships in port has climbed to 108, with container vessels accounting for 62.' Pending arrivals over the next 3 days: 42 ships, vs a 2018-2019 pre-COVID average of 37. The same report gives container dwell 'close to five days, versus 2.5 days in the first half of 2020' and 'vessel delays exceeding 7 days'.
figures.source_name: Marine Exchange of Southern California (Capt. Kip Louttit), reported by Maritime Magazine, 9 Feb 2021
figures.unit: vessels (MXSOC daily report for Monday 2021-02-08, reported 2021-02-09)
figures.value: 108 total vessels in port; 46 total vessels at anchor; 62 vessels at berth (record); container ships: 62 in port = 32 at berth (record) + 30 at anchor/drift (derived: 62 - 32)

figures.name: queue_june2021_trough
figures.notes: The mid-2021 trough between the winter 2020-21 wave and the autumn 2021 build: 'dropped to 9 in June 2021. It then increased through the late summer and fall of 2021 to a peak of 109 on 9 January 2022.' Used as the start-of-build queue level in the flow-deficit derivation (Derivation A), with 2021-06-30 as the nominal trough date — an assumption, printed there.
figures.source_name: Marine Exchange of Southern California, reported by Maritime Magazine, Nov 2022
figures.unit: container ships in the backup, June 2021 (month granularity as reported)

figures.name: queue_2021-08-29_point_count
figures.notes: MXSOC, 30 Aug 2021: '129 ships in port; 5 more than Fri & same as new record 8/29. 73 total ships at anchor... 76 container ships in the port... 47 container ships at anchor or drift area on 29 August has broken its previous record of 46 on 28 August.' Regular and contingency anchorages 'essentially full including all 10 contingency anchorages off Huntington Beach'; 11 ships in drift areas (8 container, 3 tankers). The 73 vs 75 anchor figures are the report's own two wordings (at anchor vs at anchor or in a drift area) and are kept as stated.
figures.source_name: Marine Exchange of Southern California (@MXSOCAL report of 30-31 Aug 2021), reported by Port Technology International
figures.value: 129 total ships in port (record); 73 total ships at anchor (75 at anchor/drift on 2021-08-29, record); 76 container ships in port (record); 47 container ships at anchor/drift (record, 2021-08-29)

figures.name: queue_2021-09_point_count
figures.notes: 'That day last September, there were 66 container ships crowded outside the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach... in addition to a couple of dozen unloading or transitioning in and out of berths.' Louttit: 'In a normal world, mathematically, there are supposed to be zero or one container ships at anchor.' Used as the inherited-queue level at the proposed run start (2021-10-01) in the flow-deficit derivation — the nearest documented point before 1 Oct 2021; the imprecision (day not pinned) is stated there.
figures.source_name: Marine Exchange of Southern California (Capt. Kip Louttit), reported by Marketplace (American Public Media), 29 Sep 2022, recounting its September 2021 visit
figures.unit: container ships waiting outside the ports, September 2021 (day within September not pinned by the source)

figures.name: queue_2021-10-19_point_count_and_wait
figures.notes: Chain: Western Overseas' weekly update restates the MXSOC daily report for 19 Oct 2021 verbatim in substance ('Southern California Marine Exchange reported there were a total of 159 ships in the ports of LA/LB as of October 19, 2021. This included 98 container ships with 68 at anchor or in hold areas and 30 at berth. Container vessels are waiting an average of 10-12 days to reach a terminal'). The wait is reported as a range; which endpoint is LA and which LB is not stated in the summary and is not assigned here.
figures.source_name: Marine Exchange of Southern California daily report, summarised by Western Overseas Corporation, Port Congestion Update 10/22/21
figures.value: 159 total ships in port; 98 container ships = 68 at anchor/holding areas + 30 at berth; average container-vessel wait 10-12 days

figures.name: queue_2021-11-03_point_count_and_wait
figures.notes: See queue_2021-10-19 entry for the chain and the range caveat.
figures.source_name: Marine Exchange of Southern California daily report, summarised by Western Overseas Corporation, Port Congestion Update 11/05/21
figures.value: 159 total ships in port; 102 container ships = 76 at anchorage/drift + 26 at berth/terminal; average container-vessel wait 13-14.1 days

figures.name: queue_2021-11-10_point_count_and_wait
figures.notes: The 109 here is TOTAL container ships in port on 10 Nov 2021 (79 waiting + 30 berthed) — a different quantity from the 109-ship waiting backup of 9 Jan 2022, despite the identical number. The two are never interchanged.
figures.source_name: Marine Exchange of Southern California daily report, summarised by Western Overseas Corporation, Port Congestion Update 11/12/21
figures.value: 164 total ships in port; 109 container ships = 79 at anchorage/drift + 30 at terminal/berth; average container-vessel wait 13.7-16.1 days

figures.name: queue_2021-11-16_point_count_and_wait
figures.notes: 16 Nov 2021 is the day the new queuing system for labour commenced (see new_queuing_system_start). The 86 waiting container ships on this date are corroborated independently by MXSOC's own end-of-backup statement a year later ('We went from 86 container ships anchored or loitering/drifting in our waters 16 Nov 2021...', via Port Technology International and SAFETY4SEA). 179 total vessels in port is the largest all-types in-port total sourced here.
figures.source_name: Marine Exchange of Southern California daily report, summarised by Western Overseas Corporation, Port Congestion Update 11/19/21
figures.value: 179 total vessels in port; 116 container ships = 86 at anchorage or drift + 30 at berth/terminal; average container-vessel wait 16.2-17.7 days

figures.name: new_queuing_system_start
figures.notes: From 16 Nov 2021, inbound trans-Pacific container ships took a queue place by Calculated Time of Arrival (CTA) and waited outside a Safety and Air Quality Area (SAQA) extending 150 miles west/south of Southern California (50 miles off Central/Northern California and Mexico), instead of anchoring within 40 miles. MXSOC: 'The new system didn't solve the backup but moved the backed-up container ships 50-150 miles offshore.' MEASUREMENT BREAK: backup counts before 16 Nov 2021 count ships physically at anchor/drift near the ports; counts after it count all ships in the CTA queue including slow-steaming ships across the Pacific. The two segments of the series are recorded as one documented series (as MXSOC itself reports it) but the break is flagged wherever the series is used.
figures.source_name: Marine Exchange of Southern California / Pacific Maritime Association / Pacific Merchant Shipping Association new queuing process, reported by Maritime Magazine and Port Technology International, Nov 2022

figures.name: queue_2021-11-22_conflict_pair
figures.notes: CONFLICT recorded, not blended. Both versions agree on 61 container ships physically inside the near-port area; they differ on what is added to it: A adds the 20 already waiting outside the SAQA (total backup 81, berthed ships excluded); B adds the 30 berthed ships (total container in port 91, SAQA-outside ships not in its count). Version A URL: https://maritimemag.com/en/the-huge-containership-line-ups-at-los-angeles-and-long-beach-officially-over/ . The wait range 17-19 days is from version B's summary.
figures.source_name: A: Marine Exchange of Southern California, reported by Maritime Magazine, Nov 2022. B: Marine Exchange of Southern California daily report, summarised by Western Overseas Corporation, Port Congestion Update 11/26/21
figures.value: Version A (MXSOC retrospective): backup 81 container ships = 61 inside 25/40 miles + 20 outside the SAQA. Version B (MXSOC daily report via Western Overseas): 145 total vessels; 91 container ships = 61 at anchorage/drift + 30 at berth/terminal; average wait 17-19 days

figures.name: queue_2021-12-16_point_count_and_wait
figures.notes: The same summary notes the normal alongside count is 26-31 container vessels at terminal across the twin ports, but that the Port of LA had indicated a reduced alongside count (either 4 or 5, vs its usual 18-23) since 14 Dec — recorded as reported; the summary's wording does not make clear whether that LA figure is a berth-occupancy or an arrivals figure, so it is not used in any derivation.
figures.source_name: Marine Exchange of Southern California daily report, summarised by Western Overseas Corporation, Port Congestion Update 12/17/21
figures.value: 102 container ships in the backup system = 28 anchored/loitering within 40 miles + 74 loitering/anchored outside the SAQA; average container-vessel wait 20-31 days

figures.name: queue_2021-12-27_point_count_wait_and_split
figures.notes: This is the only LA-vs-LB split of the waiting queue sourced here (anchored 5/18, loitering 38/39). One report pair on one date — recorded, but NOT generalised into a split for the whole event (see the NOT_SOURCED split entry and preregistration_v2.md §5.2 on why sea_longbeach is not shocked).
figures.source_name: Marine Exchange of Southern California (25 Dec 2021) and Port of Los Angeles Operations Report (27 Dec 2021), summarised by Western Overseas Corporation, Port Congestion Update 1/3/22
figures.value: 100 container ships in the backup system = 23 anchored within 40 miles (LA 5 + LB 18) + 77 loitering/steaming toward San Pedro Bay (LA 38 + LB 39); average container-vessel wait 20-27.3 days (Port of LA Operations Report figures, 27 Dec 2021; MXSOC count dated 25 Dec 2021 in the same summary: 97 total ships in port, 49 container ships of which 23 at anchor/loitering and 26 at berth)

figures.name: peak_backup_2022-01-09
figures.notes: PEAK QUEUE — headline figure. 'The backlog peaked on January 9, 2022, when the backlog reached 109 vessels' (Maritime Executive, reporting MXSOC). The backup counts ships WAITING for a berth; container ships alongside at berth on comparable dates numbered ~26-30 in addition (see the Nov/Dec point counts), and all-types vessels in port peaked at 179 (16 Nov 2021). Any wording that calls 109 the 'total in port' is a misreading and is corrected wherever it appears. Corroboration: Port of Long Beach February 2022 release via gCaptain: 'The containership backup at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach stood at 50 as of Thursday, down from a peak of 109 on January 9, 2022, according to the Marine Exchange of Southern California' (https://gcaptain.com/port-of-long-beach-record-february/).
figures.source_name: Marine Exchange of Southern California (Capt. Kip Louttit), reported by Maritime Executive, 22 Nov 2022; corroborated by Port Technology International and Maritime Magazine reports of the same MXSOC statement
figures.unit: container ships in the backup (waiting for berth, CTA queue incl. ships outside the SAQA) — NOT total ships in port

figures.name: near_port_loitering_zero_2022-02-03
figures.notes: 'We went from 86 container ships anchored or loitering/drifting in our waters 16 Nov 2021 first went to zero loitering on 3 February 2022 and remained at low levels subsequently.' This is the emptying of the NEAR-PORT anchor/drift areas under the SAQA system — the total CTA backup was still ~50 in mid-February 2022 (Port of Long Beach via gCaptain). It is NOT the clearance of the backup and must not be used as a clearance date.
figures.source_name: Marine Exchange of Southern California, reported by SAFETY4SEA, Nov 2022

figures.name: queue_2022-08-29_eight_ships
figures.notes: 'Eight vessels were in the official queue as of late Monday, according to data from the Marine Exchange of Southern California & Vessel Traffic Service... That's an all-time low, officials said in a statement, down from a record of 109 set in January and about 40 lined up a year ago.' First documented date at or below 10% of the peak backup (10 ships): 232 days after the 2022-01-09 peak. Used in the LB-3 observed milestones.
figures.source_name: Marine Exchange of Southern California & Vessel Traffic Service Los Angeles and Long Beach, reported by Bloomberg via AJOT (American Journal of Transportation), 30 Aug 2022
figures.unit: container ships in the official queue, as of late Monday 2022-08-29

figures.name: queue_2022-10-19_four_ships_and_berth_counts
figures.notes: 'Statistics from the Marine Exchange of Southern California show a steep drop throughout this year, from a high of 109 waiting container ships Jan. 9 to just four on Wednesday... Between August 2021 and February 2022, there were an average of 28.8 container vessels alongside in Los Angeles and Long Beach daily... The average number of ships at the ports' berths daily in full-year 2019 was 14.8.' The alongside averages are used in Derivation C with their caveat (TEU per call also rose, so alongside time is not pure service slowdown).
figures.source_name: Marine Exchange of Southern California statistics, reported by FreightWaves / American Shipper, 19 Oct 2022
figures.value: 4 container ships waiting (Wed 2022-10-19, lowest since Oct 2020); container ships alongside at berth: average 28.8/day Aug 2021-Feb 2022; average 19/day 2022-09-01 to 2022-10-18; average 14.8/day in full-year 2019 (pre-COVID)

figures.name: backup_declared_ended_2022-11-22
figures.notes: CLEARANCE — headline date. 'After 25 months, and with concurrence of the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA), and the Pacific Merchant Shipping Association (PMSA), the containership backup for the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach has ended.' On 22 Nov 2022 MXSOC reported for the first time that no container ships were waiting in the anchorage or being required to loiter offshore; on 17 Nov there had still been 3 slow-steaming in and 1 at anchor. Stated reason: 'there is ample labor to discharge and load the cargo for container ships' and carriers optimising arrivals against their CTA. Interval from the 2022-01-09 peak to this declaration: 317 days. The queue emptied over 2022 as trans-Pacific volumes fell and carriers diverted/blanked sailings — a demand-side emptying, not a dated capacity restoration (see metric LB-3).
figures.source_name: Marine Exchange of Southern California (Capt. Kip Louttit announcement, 22 Nov 2022), reported by Maritime Executive, 22 Nov 2022

figures.name: dwell_truck_san_pedro_bay_series
figures.notes: PMSA Dec 2021 release: truck dwell 'decreased slightly... On average, containers leaving on trucks remained on terminals for 7.7 days, down from 8.4 days the month before' and 'the average container dwell time for local containers leaving on trucks was under three days prior to the Covid-19 related surge'. Oct 2021 figure 7.64 days ('climbed to a record in October... up from almost 6 days in September', PMSA via Bloomberg, https://gcaptain.com/los-angeles-and-long-beach-container-dwell-times-rose-to-record-in-october/). The 2.5-day H1-2020 figure is from Maritime Magazine's 9 Feb 2021 report of PMSA/MXSOC material ('averaging close to five days, versus 2.5 days in the first half of 2020'). Jan 2023: 3.2 days, 'down from a peak of 8.4 days in November 2021' (PMSA via gCaptain, https://gcaptain.com/container-dwell-times-at-los-angeles-and-long-beach-ports-return-to-normal/). One series, one scope (truck-bound, San Pedro Bay combined) — used in Derivation B.
figures.source_name: Pacific Merchant Shipping Association (PMSA) monthly dwell releases: Oct 2021 via Bloomberg/gCaptain; Dec 2021 release on pmsaship.com; Jan 2023 via gCaptain
figures.unit: days, average container dwell on terminal for local (truck-bound) containers, San Pedro Bay ports
figures.value: Pre-surge (H1 2020 / pre-COVID): 2.5 days / 'under three days'. Oct 2021: 7.64 days. Nov 2021: 8.4 days (peak). Dec 2021: 7.7 days. Jan 2023: 3.2 days

figures.name: dwell_rail_san_pedro_bay_conflict
figures.notes: CONFLICT recorded, not blended: the October release reports rail dwell improving 'to 3.9 days from 5.5 days in September'; the December release reports rail dwell of 3.5 days in December as 'the same as October'. Both cannot hold for October. The rail series is not used in any derivation here; the discrepancy is recorded here as found.
figures.source_name: Pacific Merchant Shipping Association (PMSA), via Bloomberg/gCaptain (Oct figure) and pmsaship.com Dec 2021 release
figures.unit: days, average container dwell on terminal for rail-bound containers, San Pedro Bay ports
figures.value: Oct 2021: 3.9 days (PMSA via Bloomberg, Nov 2021). Dec 2021: 3.5 days (PMSA Dec release, whose comparison wording implies October was also 3.5 days)

figures.name: dwell_pola_import_peak_hapag_lloyd
figures.notes: 'dwell times for Port of Los Angeles import cargo has declined to 4.2 days from a peak of 11 days' (Hapag-Lloyd, via Bloomberg). A DIFFERENT series from the PMSA truck-dwell series (POLA only, import cargo generally, carrier-reported) — its 11-day peak is never blended with the PMSA 8.4-day truck peak. Recorded separately per the conflicts discipline.
figures.source_name: Hapag-Lloyd AG count, reported by Bloomberg via AJOT, 30 Aug 2022
figures.unit: days, dwell time for Port of Los Angeles import cargo (Hapag-Lloyd count as reported)
figures.value: Peak 11 days, declined to 4.2 days by late Aug 2022

figures.name: teu_2021_san_pedro_bay_record
figures.notes: Throughput ROSE to an all-time record in the congestion year — the central fact for the shock translation (shock translation): the queue formed alongside record served volume, i.e. from demand above effective capacity plus landside/productivity drag, not from a collapse in served calls. PMSA wording: 'the Port of Long Beach and Port of Los Angeles processed an all-time record high volume of 20 million TEUs in 2021' (https://www.pmsaship.com/maritime-insights-blog/san-pedro-bay-ports-dwell-time-dec-2021).
figures.source_name: Port of Los Angeles and Port of Long Beach 2021 volume releases, reported by Logistics Management; PMSA Dec 2021 dwell release
figures.value: Port of Los Angeles 10,677,609 TEU in 2021 (+13% vs 2020, new record); Port of Long Beach 9,384,368 TEU in 2021 (+15.7% vs 2020, new record); combined 20,061,977 TEU (sum as computed here); PMSA states the combined figure as '20 million TEUs in 2021, a 15.8% year-over-year increase for San Pedro Bay'

figures.name: mxsoc_full_daily_backup_series
figures.notes: The complete day-by-day MXSOC backup series was not obtained: MXSOC published daily vessel reports during the event, but no complete archived daily table was retrieved. This record uses dated point counts quoted from MXSOC daily reports by named reporting (Western Overseas weekly summaries; Port Technology International; Maritime Magazine; FreightWaves; Bloomberg via AJOT) plus MXSOC's own retrospective milestones in its 22 Nov 2022 end-of-backup announcement. No daily value has been interpolated or invented between the sourced points.
figures.unit: container ships in backup, daily, 2020-10-15 to 2022-11-22

figures.name: average_wait_on_peak_date_2022-01-09
figures.notes: Average waits are sourced for 2021-10-19 (10-12 d), 2021-11-03 (13-14.1 d), 2021-11-10 (13.7-16.1 d), 2021-11-16 (16.2-17.7 d), 2021-11-22 (17-19 d), 2021-12-16 (20-31 d) and 2021-12-27 (20-27.3 d) — but no wait figure for the peak date itself, 9 Jan 2022, was found in the sources consulted. The LB-1 conversion does not need it (the Little's-law cross-check uses the December ranges as reported, labelled as December figures).
figures.unit: days, average container-vessel wait for a berth on 2022-01-09

figures.name: la_lb_split_of_peak_backup
figures.notes: No LA-vs-LB split of the 109-ship peak backup was found. The only split sourced is for 2021-12-27 (anchored within 40 miles LA 5 / LB 18; loitering LA 38 / LB 39 — see queue_2021-12-27 entry), one date, two weeks before the peak. It is recorded but not generalised; it is one of the two stated reasons sea_longbeach is not separately shocked (preregistration_v2.md §5.2).
figures.unit: container ships waiting, split Port of Los Angeles vs Port of Long Beach, at the 2022-01-09 peak

baseline_mean_daily_import_container_ton.derivation: Mean of daily 'import_container' (AIS-estimated metric tons), port664, 2021-01-01..2021-03-31.

baseline_mean_daily_import_tonnes_ais_es.derivation: Mean of daily 'import' (all classes, AIS-estimated metric tons), port664, 2021-01-01..2021-03-31.

baseline_mean_daily_portcalls.derivation: Mean of daily 'portcalls' (all classes), port664, 2021-01-01..2021-03-31. Sum = 918.

baseline_mean_daily_portcalls_container.derivation: Mean of daily 'portcalls_container', port664, 2021-01-01..2021-03-31. Sum = 492. This is the LB-1 conversion rate.

baseline_window.derivation: Earliest full quarter in the stored series, used as the baseline. CAVEAT, stated plainly: this baseline is already congested (MXSOC backup was ~30-42 container ships in Feb 2021). The stored window contains no uncongested quarter — the backup ran continuously from Oct 2020 — so every PortWatch change below is peak-vs-early-congestion, not peak-vs-normal. No pre-congestion PortWatch baseline is computed here.

import_container_tonnes_change_pct_peak_.derivation: 100 x (310107.27 - 331538.62) / 331538.62. The largest PortWatch decline in the peak window is in container import tonnage (-6.5%), on slightly MORE container calls (+3.7%) — i.e. less estimated import tonnage per container call, not fewer calls.

import_tonnes_change_pct_peak_vs_baselin.derivation: 100 x (429946.32 - 435144.39) / 435144.39. All-class AIS-estimated import tonnage essentially flat (-1.2%).

peak_backup_days_of_flow_all_calls.derivation: 109 / 10.200 (baseline all-class calls/day) = 10.69 days of flow. Printed for the record only: it divides a container-only queue by an all-class flow and is NOT the LB-1 comparator (preregistration_v2.md §5.2 states why).

peak_backup_days_of_flow_container.derivation: 109 (MXSOC peak backup, 2022-01-09) / 5.467 (baseline container calls/day) = 19.94 days of flow. LB-1 observed comparator. Cross-check with the peak-window rate: 109 / 5.667 = 19.23 days — and Little's law then predicts a mean wait of ~19.2 days, against documented December average waits of 20-31 days (16 Dec) and 20-27.3 days (27 Dec). Same order; the December wait ranges are December figures, not a January measurement (see NOT_SOURCED wait entry).

peak_mean_daily_import_container_tonnes_.derivation: Mean of daily 'import_container' (AIS-estimated metric tons), port664, 2021-10-01..2022-01-31.

peak_mean_daily_import_tonnes_ais_estima.derivation: Mean of daily 'import' (all classes, AIS-estimated metric tons), port664, 2021-10-01..2022-01-31.

peak_mean_daily_portcalls.derivation: Mean of daily 'portcalls' (all classes), port664, 2021-10-01..2022-01-31. Sum = 1351.

peak_window.derivation: The documented peak-queue window: MXSOC waiting counts run 68 (19 Oct) through the 109 peak (9 Jan) across exactly this span.

portcalls_change_pct_peak_vs_baseline.derivation: 100 x (10.984 - 10.200) / 10.200. POSITIVE: total port calls ROSE in the peak window. There is no PortWatch call drop to grade — see metric LB-2.
